versions.description: Posts holds three things. A channel is one account this project publishes as — which network, whose account, where inside it the posts go where the network needs telling, and a credential kept in this machine's vault under a name the record carries, never in the record itself. A draft is what the project is about to say, written for one channel, with the room left in it counted down as somebody writes. A publication is what it said, carrying the text exactly as it went out and the identifier the network issued, so editing a draft afterwards cannot rewrite the account of it. All three are ordinary records: they live in the project's memory, travel with the repository, and can be written or read by an agent as easily as by a person — while the credential stays on the machine and travels nowhere. Publishing is a person's act: they read the exact text and press the button, there is no clock in here, and nothing sends anything while nobody is looking. Four networks are reached from this window — LinkedIn, Bluesky, Threads and Telegram — and a Telegram channel says what it is: a bot posting into a chat, not a person speaking.
versions.changelog:
Archiving the draft says how.

The step after a post goes out is *archive the draft*, and nothing said what
that is: the flag was not on Sync's write when this was written, so an agent
following the instruction either left the draft where it was or set a product
field of its own invention. It is `archived: true` on the record, in the write
that files the publication.

versions.description: Posts holds three things. A channel is one account this project publishes as — which network, whose account, where inside it the posts go where the network needs telling, and a credential kept in this machine's vault under a name the record carries, never in the record itself. A draft is what the project is about to say, written for one channel, with the room left in it counted down as somebody writes. A publication is what it said, carrying the text exactly as it went out and the identifier the network issued, so editing a draft afterwards cannot rewrite the account of it. All three are ordinary records: they live in the project's memory, travel with the repository, and can be written or read by an agent as easily as by a person — while the credential stays on the machine and travels nowhere. Publishing is a person's act: they read the exact text and press the button, there is no clock in here, and nothing sends anything while nobody is looking. Four networks are reached from this window — LinkedIn, Bluesky, Threads and Telegram — and a Telegram channel says what it is: a bot posting into a chat, not a person speaking.

Posts holds two things and reaches nothing. A draft is what the project is about to say, written for one named network — the section knows how long a post may be there and who may read one, and counts down while somebody writes. A publication is what it said, carrying the text exactly as it went out, so editing a draft afterwards cannot rewrite the account of it. Both are ordinary records: they live in the project's memory, travel with the repository, and can be written or read by an agent as easily as by a person. Sending is deliberately not here. Sync has no connection to any network and stores no account for one; pressing Publish hands the post to an agent, which delivers it with a tool somebody connected to that agent — an MCP server for that network. So this section is worth installing where an agent has hands, and where one has not, it is a good place to write and a place that will tell you plainly that nothing can go out. Publishing is a person's act either way: there is no clock in here, and nothing that sends anything while nobody is looking.
